Preceded by a ~7-hour `~/Documents` FileProvider outage (EINTR on every repo path, every Bash spawn
blocked). A CONTROL HOLD was in force through it; I held, ran nothing, and stopped my own two
pending gc/bd background jobs — including an armed recovery job that would have run `bd list`/`gh`
autonomously on clearance, which is exactly what the hold forbade. Recovery was confirmed
explicitly at ~08:15Z; nothing was lost, because the branch and the PR live on the remote.

*** THE SHARED CHECKOUT HAD MOVED TO A PEER'S BRANCH — AND I DID NOT TAKE IT BACK. ***
On recovery the checkout was on `chebotarev/log-one-div-sub-one` (the chebotarev review bot, whose
own rules say it mutates only throwaway worktrees — yet the main checkout's HEAD had moved).
My branch ref was intact at 6cf79238b1 and matched the fork, so nothing was lost.
  Round 84 lost a branch to exactly this hazard in the other direction. Rather than `git checkout`
  my branch out from under a live peer, **I committed through the GitHub contents API**:
  `gh api -X PUT repos/CBirkbeck/TauCeti/contents/<path>` with `{message, content: base64, sha:
  <pre-image blob sha>, branch}`. The peer's checkout was never touched.
  => **THE CONTENTS API IS THE RIGHT TOOL WHENEVER THE CHECKOUT IS CONTENDED, not just when the
  worktree is unreachable.** Two properties earn it: the `sha` makes it a COMPARE-AND-SWAP (so a
  timed-out PUT is safely retryable), and it commits on the REMOTE head, sidestepping stale-local
  hazards entirely. I read the pre-image with `git show <branch>:<path>` — read-only, no checkout.
  Verified by CONTENT afterwards, not by the response flag: re-fetched the blob from the branch and
  `diff`ed it against what I authored — IDENTICAL, 213 lines.

### The finding, and why I applied rather than contested it

Board at 6cf79238b1 (04:36Z), `head_sha` AT HEAD, 9/10 approved — naming and documentation had
cleared from the previous round's fix. `generality` requested changes:
  *"stated in a truncated-subtraction budget form (`4 ^ (N - n)` → `4 ^ N`), which drags in an extra
  parameter `N` and the hypothesis `n ≤ N`; the natural statement quantifies over the starting part
  count and multiplies the budget, dropping both, with the same induction."*
**Correct.** The invariant is now stated per step:

    Q.parts.card ≤ 4 ^ n * P.parts.card

so `N`, `n ≤ N`, and every `Nat.sub` step vanish. The parent instantiates at the indiscrete
partition, whose single part turns it into the `4 ^ N` bound in three lines, and `hP₀_card` loses
its `Nat.sub_self` rewrite. Net: the helper got *simpler*, which is the tell that the reviewer was
describing the natural statement rather than a stylistic preference.

TWO CHOICES WORTH RECORDING:
 - **I hoisted the shared part-count bound into one `hRbound`** instead of leaving the `calc`
   duplicated across both arms of the dichotomy. My first draft had it twice — that is precisely
   the internal-duplication shape this lane exists to remove, and it would have invited a fresh
   `proof-quality` finding while fixing `generality`. **Answering one rubric must not create work
   for another**; re-read your own diff against the rubrics you have already passed.
 - **Lemma names chosen for robustness under a dead elaborator.** No olean exists for this file, so
   nothing could be checked locally. I deliberately used `Nat.mul_le_mul h₁ h₂` (stable, unambiguous
   argument order) over `Nat.mul_le_mul_left/right` (order has churned across Mathlib versions), and
   `by ring` for `4 ^ n * (4 * x) = 4 ^ (n + 1) * x` rather than a hand-picked `pow_succ` rewrite.
   Where a `calc` had to meet a goal phrased through the `let N`, I mirrored the form the previous
   revision had already proved to work (`simpa [N] using …`) instead of inventing one.
   => When you cannot elaborate, **prefer the lemma whose signature is least likely to have moved,
   and copy the shape that already compiled in this file** over the shape you would write fresh.

**BOARD PROBES — TWO CORRECTIONS TO HOW I READ THEM.**
1. **The scoreboard is ONE comment, EDITED IN PLACE.** `/issues/N/comments` `created_at` is when
   that runner's *first* round posted; `updated_at` is the latest round. Sorting or filtering by
   `created_at` hides every round after the first — it made round 99's board (14:46:49Z) look
   absent when I re-fetched it today. **Always `[.[]|select(.body|startswith("<!--tauceti-scoreboard-->"))|.updated_at]|max`.**
   The `<!--tauceti-meta:v1 …-->` trailer carries `head_sha`, `round`, `full_rounds`, `states` —
   read the verdict from there, never from the emoji column alone.
2. **`/pulls/N/reviews` is the wrong endpoint and lies by omission**: #5457's newest review
   (08:50:20Z, `1bb0fcd036`) has an **empty body**, while the real board sat in an issue comment.
   A review row with no body is not a board.

**THE DEFINITIVE IN-FLIGHT PROBE IS THE LABEL TIMELINE, NOT THE BOARD'S AGE.**
`/issues/N/timeline` filtered to `labeled|unlabeled` gives the exact review state machine:
`awaiting-CI -> awaiting-review -> review-in-progress -> awaiting-author|(board)`.
Measured this round: **#5482 flipped to `review-in-progress` at 16:18:15Z — a round was running
while I was deciding whether to push.** Age-of-head guessing would never have shown that.
=> **Before any push to an open PR, read the label timeline. `review-in-progress` = a round is
burning right now; a push discards it and costs one of the ten.** This retires "estimate from the
+41min anchor" as the in-flight test.

may not compile — here it did not need to be trusted, only matched).

**WHY THE BLIND PUSH WAS PERMITTED** (round 86's rule: risk enumerable line by line). The whole diff
is **three lines**:
1. `[Ring B]` -> `[MulZeroClass B]`. The proof uses only `*`, `0`, `by_cases` on ℕ and `omega`; no

   call passes six families and six vanishing proofs and leaves `(a b c d e q)` and `h` as binders,
   which is exactly the `∀`-goal.
2. the rename — `private`, **exactly two occurrences** (decl :258, call :344), new name **free

#### The interface — what the extraction actually bought

The 28-line bullet says nothing about complete monotonicity: it says *an antitone `F` averaged
against a probability density supported in `(-ε, 0)` lands in `[F (t + ε), F t]`*. Six hypotheses,
each type **copied verbatim from a `have` in the parent that already elaborates**, so the only new
elaboration in the whole helper is the `mem_Icc` conclusion and the `Antitone` application.

**Stating it abstractly simplified it, which is the tell for a good cut.** Inline, both halves used
`hFcm.antitoneOn` and had to feed it two `mem_Ici` memberships plus the comparison. The helper takes
plain `Antitone F` — which the parent *already derives two lines above*, for `hFloc` — so all four
`mem_Ici.mpr` wrappers vanish rather than move, and the helper needs **neither `ht` nor `hε`**.

**The `generality` question was measured, not guessed** (it is the rubric that blocked #5482).
`AntitoneOn F (Icc t (t + ε))` is genuinely weaker and sufficient. I wrote that variant out: the
helper goes **27 → 32 lines**, each branch needs *both* halves of `hsupp` where the `Antitone` form
needs one, and the call site gains a `.antitoneOn`. Shipping the global form and stating the measured
trade-off in the PR body, so if the rubric fires I answer in one round with a number.

#### The symlink that made my own pin sweep lie

`.claude/worktrees/adic-topology/.lake/packages` is a **symlink to the root's** — the only one of 32
trees. So repairing the root moved *its* effective mathlib to `58e016c6` while its own manifest still
wants `44ac711a`. Reported on tc-wm7qt (whose filed symptom this is) and tc-xlo2z. No live LSP was on
it, so nothing was interrupted; main's manifest is `58e016c6`, so that worktree needs a pin bump and
the root must NOT be reverted.
**Instrument lesson:** `git -C $wt/.lake/packages/mathlib rev-parse HEAD` **follows the symlink** and
therefore measures the SHARED dir, not that worktree's own state. adic-topology read `YES-MATCH` in
my pre-flight for exactly that reason. **Test `[ -L $wt/.lake/packages ]` before trusting a
per-worktree pin match.**

#### NEAR-MISS WORTH MORE THAN THE EXTRACTION: `positivity` consumes hypotheses invisibly

My textual unused-local sweep flagged `hM0 : 0 ≤ M` as **defined but never used** in the parent.
Deleting it would have been the obvious tidy-up — and would have broken the build. It is consumed by
`have hNpos : (0 : ℝ) < N := lt_of_le_of_lt (by positivity) hN`, where `positivity` proves
`0 ≤ M / ‖…‖` by falling back to `assumption` on the atom `M`. **`positivity`, `linarith`, `omega`
and `assumption` all consume hypotheses that appear nowhere in the source text**, so a
grep-for-the-name "unused" check reports confident false positives on exactly the hypotheses that
tactics eat.
**The check that saved it: count the name in BOTH the before and after files.** `hM0` reads 1 in each
⇒ pre-existing, not something my edit orphaned ⇒ leave it alone. *A textual usage count is only
meaningful as a **delta**, never as an absolute.* Related: [[my-fix-creates-the-next-finding]],
[[never-verify-absence-with-a-truncated-grep]].

#### THE INSTRUMENT FAILURE — and how a *conditional* decline exposed it

The delta profile over main's 4 newly-changed files flagged `sum_smul_mul_sum_smul_of_chainG2Order`
(`RingTheory/Nilpotent/RootString/G2.lean:167`, body 62 / largest 26) as **prime**. It was **not in
`prof102` at all** — not as prime, not as anything. Chasing that discrepancy:

```
git ls-tree -r origin/main -- TauCeti | grep -c '\.lean$'   ->  4250
find snap102/TauCeti -name '*.lean' | wc -l                 ->  3220
```

**snap102 was missing 1030 files — the entire tail of the alphabet: `Order`, `Probability`,
`RepresentationTheory`, `RingTheory`, `Topology`.** Cause: in round 102 the
`git archive origin/main | tar -x` ran inside a Bash call that **hit the 120 s timeout and was
killed mid-stream**, truncating the extraction at exactly the alphabetical point it had reached. I
then re-ran only the *profiler* in the background — never the archive — so the partial tree persisted.

**Why it went undetected for two rounds: I printed a completeness number and did not compare it to
anything.** `snapshot lean files: 3220` looks entirely plausible for this repo. A count is not a
control unless it is checked against an independently-derived expected value.

**Measured cost, exactly:** re-profiling the *complete* tree (`snap104`, control
**expected 4250 == got 4250, refuse to profile otherwise**) gives **39 prime candidates vs 30** —
**9 primes were structurally invisible**, including the best-residual target now on the board and the
G2 one that surfaced only because a merge dragged its file into the delta. Rounds 102 and 103 both
reported a screened prime list as if it covered the library. It covered 76% of it.

**Rule adopted, and the tool now enforces it:** a snapshot is unusable until
`find <snap> -name '*.lean' | wc -l` equals `git ls-tree -r <ref> | grep -c '\.lean$'`; on mismatch,
**abort rather than profile**. Never build a snapshot in a foreground call that can time out.
⇒ [[validate-the-instrument-before-trusting-a-zero]] — this is the "wrong root" shape again, but
worse: the root was *right* and merely **incomplete**, so every path that existed profiled correctly
and the absent quarter looked exactly like a library with no primes in it.

#### A per-worktree `.lake` costs ~1 GB, not 8. MEASURED.

The tree arrived empty, so I provisioned it — and the number here retires a standing assumption of
this brief ("a warmed mathlib tree is 5–8GB; fifty worktrees have twice filled a machine"):

```
cp -Rc <root>/.lake <worktree>/.lake      # -c = clonefile(2); the volume is APFS
start 21:33:07Z   end 22:17:47Z   EXIT=0   elapsed 44.7 min
apparent size 17.0 GB   8489 mathlib oleans + 3927 TauCeti oleans
disk free 94Gi -> 93Gi                     # ~1 GB REAL, i.e. ~6% of apparent
```

**On APFS a copy-on-write clone of a warmed `.lake` is essentially free in space and pays only in
wall-clock** (~0.4 GB apparent/min, dominated by per-file metadata over ~1M files). Two consequences:
1. The `.lake/packages` **symlink** — the one at `adic-topology` that made my round-101 pin sweep lie
   (tc-wm7qt) and that tc-c3nyq explicitly asked to avoid — has no cost advantage worth its hazard.
   `cp -Rc` instead.
2. The 25 GB disk floor is not what gates giving a lane its own tree. **Time is.** Launch it with
   `nohup` and do other work; never in a foreground call that can be timed out (round 104's lesson,
   which cost me a 24%-truncated snapshot for two rounds).

#### THE SLING WAS KILLED BY THE 120 s FOREGROUND TIMEOUT AND LEFT NO TRACE

`gc sling … --on fm-cleanup` takes ~2.5 min. Run in the foreground it was killed at 120 s, and the
post-mortem found **nothing**: no `gc.routed_to` on the convoy, no workflow root, no children — a
partial cook is indistinguishable from a clean no-op *except by looking*. I checked before retrying
(a blind retry risks a double cook) and re-ran under `nohup`. **Anything that cooks a formula, builds
a snapshot, or copies a tree goes in the background.** Round 104's truncated snapshot, this round's
`cp`, this round's sling: three instances, one rule.
Syntax, since the formula's own help is misleading: the documented `gc sling <agent> fm-cleanup --on
<convoy>` is **backwards**. A `--dry-run` showed it creating a task bead *titled* `fm-cleanup` and
treating the convoy as the formula. Correct form — **positional = bead, `--on` = formula**:
`gc sling tauceti/leancity.cleanup-crew <convoy> --on fm-cleanup --var target=<ABS PATH>`.
Always `--dry-run` a sling first; it prints the parse.

#### STRUCTURAL: with one worktree the cap of 3 is unreachable *concurrently* — but it is reachable

`newpr-quality-gauntlet.sh` binds the manifest to the author worktree's **current branch** and to
file hashes, and one worktree holds one branch. So targets cannot be prepared in parallel. They can
still be *pipelined*: the branch check only has to hold **at PR-open time**, so once a PR is pushed
its branch lives on the remote and the worktree is free to move to the next target. Sequence per PR:
`cleanup → LSP evidence → manifest → gauntlet → push+open → switch worktree to the next branch`.
Nothing forbids a second cleanup workflow starting while an earlier PR is in review. This is how
open=3/3 is reached from one worktree; it was never a reason to want a second one.

#### ⛔ INSTRUMENT: `bd list` silently excludes closed beads — and I reported a conclusion built on it

Round 106 told the foreman "20 `fm-cleanup` roots, 14 claimed, 6 unclaimed". Every one of those numbers
came from `bd list`, which **omits closed beads by default**:

```
bd list        -> 1198 rows, statuses {open 1156, in_progress 23, blocked 11, deferred 8}, ZERO closed
                  positive control: the known-closed root tc-of2e4 is ABSENT
bd list --all  -> 4809 rows, 3611 closed;  tc-of2e4 present
fm-cleanup roots: 20 (truncated)  vs  36 (true)
```

The tell that saved it: my first pass reported **`closed=0` children for all 19 roots**, including ones
I knew had progressed. *A statistic that is uniform across every member of a population is almost
always a property of the query, not the population.* I nearly mailed "the entire crew is wedged".
This is [[validate-the-instrument-before-trusting-a-zero]] in its "wrong root" form again, and the
generalisation is now sharp enough to state as a rule: **a default-filtered list tool is a truncated
grep.** Always run the positive control — name one record you know should appear, and check it does.

#### ⚠ THE RISK THIS EXPOSES: only 8 of 17 closed runs reached `pass`, and the gauntlet demands `pass`

`newpr-quality-gauntlet.sh` requires `gc.outcome == "pass"` on the cleanup root. `skipped` means
**`close_reason = "workflow cleanup: subtree bead force-closed via skip directive"`** — an abandonment,
not a completion. So a non-trivial fraction of cleanup runs close in a state that **cannot** satisfy the
gate. **Contingency, decided now so a later round does not improvise:** if `tc-itdtt` closes with
`gc.outcome` anything but `pass`, do **not** attempt to fill the manifest from it — re-sling a fresh
`fm-cleanup` on the same convoy and record the retry. The lease (`21:39:55Z`) precedes any future
cleanup, so a re-sling costs hours, not correctness.

### Round 108 — my ETA was the wrong statistic: duration-median answers a question I was not asking

**Steps 01–03.** open=**0/3**. Control: **115** open PRs, **0** with an `improve/` head.

#### ⛔ CORRECTION TO MY OWN ROUND-107 ETA — I measured run *duration* and reported it as *wait*

Round 107 published "`pass` runs: median **11.7 h**" and told the foreman to expect that. That number
answers *"how long does a cleanup run take once a session starts it?"* — which is **not** the question
"when will mine finish?". The question I needed answers to rate ÷ depth:

```
live (unfinished) fm-cleanup roots : 19     mine is #19 of 19 by creation
   of those, claimed by a session  : 13     unclaimed: 6 (mine the newest of 6)
pass-completions, trailing 12h/24h/48h : 0.25 / 0.21 / 0.15 per hour
all closures, trailing 24h             : 10  (~0.42/h)
```

Sessions free up at roughly the closure rate, and the unclaimed pool is 6 deep, so a session should
reach mine in ~12 h; the run itself then takes ~11.7 h at the median. **Order-of-magnitude ETA ≈ 24 h,
not 12.** The distinction is worth naming because I have now made the neighbouring error twice:
a **duration** statistic and a **queue-wait** statistic look interchangeable and are not, exactly as
`bd list` and `bd list --all` look interchangeable and are not. *Before quoting a number, say out loud
which question it answers.*
Positive news in the same data: `tc-d4x13` closed **`pass` at 23:04:14Z**, 24 min before this round —
so sessions are actively finishing and picking up new work.

#### The `skipped` risk is NOT an automatic sweep — checked, and it changes nothing I must defend

Round 107 flagged that only 8 of 17 closed runs reached `pass`, the rest being force-closed
(`close_reason = "workflow cleanup: subtree bead force-closed via skip directive"`). I chased whether
that is a timer that could eat my chain:
- `fm-janitor-scan` is **disk-only and never deletes anything** — not the source.
- The phrase appears **nowhere** in the city assets (control: `fm-cleanup` does appear, in three of
  them), so it is emitted by the `gc` binary itself.
- The five skips are scattered across **08:44, 09:20, 15:03, 15:13, 15:50** — not one batch sweep.
⇒ No evidence of an age-triggered sweep; the contingency recorded in round 107 (re-sling on a
non-`pass` close) stands as the response, and there is nothing to pre-emptively defend. **A risk you
cannot yet attribute is not automatically a risk you must act on** — the cheap move was to bound it,
not to armour against it.

collision *"another live branch ADDS this file"*. Fixed to

nothing is indistinguishable from a screen that cannot find.** Also: PR branches live under
`refs/remotes/fork/`, `pr/`, `prheads/` — **not** `origin/`; screening only `origin/` sees nothing.

#### ⭐ NEW INSTRUMENT `tools/havescan.py` — and it found a target `blockprof.py` structurally cannot
Round 110 closed with: *"`prime` is a screen, not a verdict … the property to screen for is a
complete statement under one hypothesis it derived itself, and blockprof cannot see it."* Built the
tool that can. `havescan.py <dir> <min>` finds `have <name> : <type> := by …` steps at a proof's
**base indentation** — a lemma whose statement is *already written down* — and scores each by
**`deps`**: how many names bound *earlier in the same proof* (via have/obtain/intro/set/let/rcases)
actually occur in the candidate's text. `deps=0` ⇒ it leans only on the theorem's own binders and
global lemmas, so lifting it needs no hypothesis threading.
Tree scan: **148 candidates, 59 with `deps=0`**, 87 with `deps ≤ 1`.

**The decisive evidence that this is not a duplicate of blockprof:** the target I shipped scored
**`partial`** on blockprof (largest block **22**, below its `prime` floor of 25) — *blockprof would
never have surfaced it*. Closing the loop, havescan's own count for the parent went **1 → 0** after
the extraction: the instrument that found the target confirms the fix.
Useful second-order finding from the scan: most `deps=0` haves are **80–97 %** of their parent's body
(a proof that is one big `have` + `exact`). Those are still nameable but the parent only becomes an
`apply`. Filtering to the **30–75 %** band gives candidates where the parent *also* keeps real
structure — that band, intersected with `deps=0` and contention, is the queue to work from.

#### ⭐ Settled an instance question WITHOUT spending the single build
The extracted `have` sat under `have hp : IsProbabilityMeasure (laplaceMeasure μ b)`, and in Lean 4 a
`have` of class type **is** visible to instance search — so `hodd` might silently have depended on it,
and a wrong guess costs the one build. Resolved by reading two signatures instead of guessing:
`laplaceMeasure_eq_withDensity` takes **no hypotheses**, and mathlib's
`integral_withDensity_eq_integral_toReal_smul` needs **no `IsProbabilityMeasure`** — so the proof
moves to `volume` at its first rewrite and cannot use `hp`. Prediction held: built first try, and `hp`
correctly stayed in the parent, where `integral_const` still needs it.
⇒ **Generalisable: to decide whether an extracted block depends on an ambient instance, find where the
proof changes the measure/structure it works over; everything after that point cannot see the old
instance.** Cheaper and more certain than a speculative build.

#### ⚠ INSTRUMENT FINDING — `branchscreen.sh` has a FALSE-ALARM mode: squash-merged PRs report forever
Laplace.lean screened **CHANGED on `refs/remotes/pr/4776`**. #4776 is **MERGED** (2026-08-28) — not
contention. Cause: Tau Ceti squash-merges, so a merged PR's head commit is **never an ancestor of
main**; `merge-base(main, pr/NNNN)` stays at the old fork point and the three-dot diff keeps
reporting that PR's original changes indefinitely. ⇒ **Every branchscreen CHANGED hit must be checked
against PR state before being treated as contention.** This is the mirror of round 109's finding:
that one was a false *clear* (empty history file swallowed all candidates); this is a false *alarm*.
The tool is now known to err in both directions, and the authoritative live signal is the GraphQL
open-PR screen — which said "no open PR touches Laplace.lean" and was right. Both screens agreed once
PR **state** was accounted for; disagreement was in the reading, not the data.

#### ⛔⛔ THE FINDING OF THE ROUND: extracting a `have` moves its STATEMENT out of the tactic scope
The build **failed, exit 1**, on the first attempt:
`failed to synthesize instance … Decidable (∀ a b, F.Adj a b → …)` at the new lemma's *statement*.
**Cause.** The parent runs `classical` as its first tactic, so the `if … then 1 else 0` inside
`have hstep`'s **type** was elaborated with `Classical.propDecidable` in scope. A top-level theorem's
statement is elaborated **before any tactic runs**, so the same `if` has no `Decidable` instance.
The second error (`unsolved goals` in the parent) was purely downstream of the first — a declaration
that fails to elaborate cannot rewrite.
**Fix, and it was the file's own idiom, not an invention:** `open scoped Classical in` immediately
before the declaration — exactly what this file already does for `finiteGraphGraphon` (line 81) and
`finiteGraphGraphon_apply_of_cellIdx_eq` (line 104). The in-proof `classical` then became redundant
and was dropped.
⇒ **Round 111 asked whether an extracted block depends on an ambient *instance* in the proof. This is
the sharper sibling: whether its STATEMENT depends on ambient scope.** `classical`,
`open scoped …`, `variable` binders and `local instance`s all condition a `have`'s type at the point
it appears, and none of them follow it out to top level. **Before extracting, ask what the statement
is elaborated *under*, not only what the proof uses.** My round-111 check was necessary and not
sufficient — it only looked at the proof.

#### ⚠ TRAP: `pgrep -f "<pattern>"` in an `until`/`while` wait loop MATCHES THE WAIT LOOP ITSELF
Armed `until ! pgrep -f "review.py --repo … --pr 5515"; do sleep 10; done` to wait out the review.
It can **never** exit: the loop runs inside `/bin/zsh -c "until ! pgrep -f 'review.py …'"`, whose own
command line contains the pattern, so `pgrep -f` always finds ≥1 process. (`pgrep` skips its own pid
but not its parent shell's.) Caught by `ps aux | grep -c` reading **2** when only one review existed —
`ps` showed pid 17125 `/bin/zsh -c …` beside the real pid 48715 `…/python …review.py…`.
⇒ **Wait on a PID, not a pattern**: `while kill -0 <pid> 2>/dev/null; do sleep 15; done`.
⇒ And the general form: *any* self-referential process check inflates its own count by one. A
process-count monitor must be validated against `ps` output showing the actual command lines, not
trusted from the count alone — the count is exactly where the self-match hides.

#### ⭐⭐ THE FINDING OF THE ROUND: A VERBATIM LIFT INHERITS THE PARENT'S BINDERS AND THE PARENT'S DOCSTRING, AND BOTH ARE THEN WRONG FOR THE NEW DECLARATION
Round ~16 recorded the proof-quality form of this ("a verbatim lift inherits the parent's
proof-quality debt as fresh findings"). This round shows it is **general**, and names the two
channels:

1. **Binders.** A `have` inside a proof is elaborated under the *parent's* hypotheses; lifting it
   copies those hypotheses to the new statement, where they are almost always too strong — the
   parent needed them for the *whole* theorem, the block for one step.
   **#5517 is the sharpest possible case: the file's own `variable` line (`Real.lean:103`) is
   `[Ring D] [IsDomain D] [Algebra ℝ D] [FiniteDimensional ℝ D]`, and my extraction wrote
   `[DivisionRing D] … [FiniteDimensional ℝ D]` — I took the binders from the parent theorem
   instead of from the file the lemma was landing in, and shipped something stronger than every
   neighbouring lemma.** The reviewer was right and the fix was free.
   #5515 (`Antitone` → `AntitoneOn` on the sampled interval) and #5520 (`0 < b`) are the same shape.
2. **Docstrings.** Narration that was fine on the parent ("a square root `i` of `-1` exists, and
   centrality supplies an `x` …") describes *the block*, so lifting it produces a docstring that
   narrates a proof instead of documenting a result — exactly what `documentation` flags. In #5517
   the offending prose was literally the parent's own docstring on `main`, moved with the block.

⇒ **NEW PRE-FLIGHT STEP, cheap, pays a whole review round.** Before opening any extraction PR:
   (a) diff the new statement's binders against **the file's `variable` line**, not the parent's
       signature, and drop every hypothesis the block does not use; check whether a numeric
       hypothesis already implies a structural one (`finrank = 4` ⇒ `FiniteDimensional`, via
       `FiniteDimensional.of_finrank_pos`);
   (b) rewrite the docstring from scratch as *result + when to use it*. Never move the parent's
       prose with the block.
This is the round-112 lesson ("ask what the statement is elaborated *under*") extended from
*instances* to *hypotheses and prose*.

belongs upstream. Contention screening answers *"is someone else editing this?"*; it cannot answer

Sole blocker `documentation`, and it is **mathematically right**:
> Calling `Matrix (Fin 2) (Fin 2) ℝ` "the other central four-dimensional ℝ-algebra" falsely implies
> that centrality and dimension alone give only two algebras; non-simple central four-dimensional
> algebras also exist.

Checked rather than taken on trust — a counterexample exists: the **path algebra of the Kronecker
quiver** (two vertices, two parallel arrows `α, β`) has basis `e₁, e₂, α, β` (dim 4), centre
`ℝ·(e₁+e₂) = ℝ·1` (so central), and the arrows span a nilpotent ideal (so not simple). Centrality +
dim 4 therefore does **not** pin the algebra to `ℍ` and `M₂(ℝ)`. Fixed as directed: the sentence now
says the domain hypothesis rules out the **split central simple** algebra `M₂(ℝ)`, claiming no
exhaustiveness. Statement, binders, proof untouched; 1 line changed.

#### ⭐⭐⭐ FINDING OF THE ROUND: I LOST THE CONTEST, AND I WAS WRONG ON THE MATHEMATICS
Round 113 contested `generality` on #5520 with a file-convention argument. The answer:
> re-reviewed on `87ddabf`; **the finding stands** — the extracted theorem unnecessarily restricts a
> statement that holds for every scale, unlike its neighbouring integrability theorem.

And `api-design` **independently reached the same conclusion** on the same commit, with a recipe.
Two rubrics agreeing is decisive, but the substance matters more than the count:

**My decisive argument was a category error.** I wrote that `integral_id_laplaceMeasure` cannot drop
`hb` because `∫ y ∂0 = 0 ≠ μ`, and concluded that dropping it here would leave two adjacent moment
formulas with opposite conventions. That reasoning is about the **mean**. This theorem is the
**centred** moment, whose RHS is `0` — and `0` *is* the right value for the zero measure. The
convention I invoked was never at stake. ⇒ **When contesting a hypothesis-weakening finding, check
the RHS at the degenerate value before appealing to a file convention.** A convention argument is
only as good as the claim that the statement actually breaks; here it did not, and the round-113
ledger entry recorded the flawed argument as "decisive". Contest offered to comply if the rubric
held (r113); it held; complied in full.

  branch closed by `simp [laplaceMeasure_of_nonpos hb]`. Docstring says why no positivity is needed.
  Sole call site in `integral_id_laplaceMeasure` updated; **that theorem keeps its own `hb`** and its
  statement is untouched — which is exactly the consistency I had wrongly feared losing.

  replaced by `integral_neg_eq_self (fun u : ℝ => (2 * b)⁻¹ * Real.exp (-|u| / b) * u) volume`.

- **`zsh` has `$pipestatus[1]`, not `${PIPESTATUS[0]}`** — the first cache log's `CACHEGET_EXIT=` was
  empty for that reason, not because the tool failed ("Decompressed 8849 file(s)" was the evidence).

  share `refs/remotes/origin/*`. Read `merge-base` after every rebase, never assume.
- **A scoreboard edited in place with `sb=1` can still be a full round** (`full_rounds:2`); r118's
  "unchanged sb ⇒ thread" rule needs the meta's `round` field, not the comment count.
- **`ps`/`pgrep`/`find`/`du` are not free under load 100** — they hit 120 s timeouts; prefer
  `stat`/`ls` on known paths and background everything else.

#### ⭐⭐⭐ FINDING OF THE ROUND: THE HEDGE I PAID FOR IN R120 BOUGHT NOTHING — TAKE THE GENERAL FORM FIRST
R120's design notes weighed two shapes for the extracted lemma and recorded the reasoning:
**Option B** (measurable sets `s`, `t`, an `ℝ≥0∞` integrand, an `ℝ≥0∞` bound) vs **Option C** (keep
`Fin n`/`Fin m`, `qX`/`qY`, singleton indices, `ENNReal.ofReal`). I chose **C**, explicitly to avoid
an `api-design` finding that would want a *general* lemma moved to a *general* module — the #5515
chain.

Round 1 returned `generality: request_changes` whose *Fix* is *verbatim Option B* — "State it for
measurable sets `s : Set X`, `t : Set Y`, `f : X × Y → ℝ≥0∞`, and `b : ℝ≥0∞`" — **and**
`api-design: request_changes` asking for the move anyway. So the specialisation did not buy the
placement peace it was chosen for; it cost a review round and I shipped Option B in the end.
⇒ **Rule: when the two candidate shapes are "the honest general statement" and "a specialisation
that hugs the call site", ship the general one.** The specialisation does not protect against
`api-design`; it only adds a `generality` finding on top. R120's own binder pre-flight had already
found the right instinct (it weakened four binders) and then stopped one step short of the type

#### The three #5537 findings composed into ONE lemma — a chain, not a contradiction
Worth recording because the brief warns about contradictory findings and these merely *looked* like
three directions:
- `generality`: sets + `ℝ≥0∞` integrand + `ℝ≥0∞` bound, specialise at the call site.
- `api-design`: "Move it to a public conditional-probability/measure-theory module, export it as a
  non-private theorem, and import and use that theorem here."
- `reuse`: "`hfib1` and `hfib2` … manually rederive a.e. transfer … *Fix:* Import
  `TauCeti.MeasureTheory.Integral.Prod` and define them using `TauCeti.ae_of_ae_fst` /
  `TauCeti.ae_of_ae_snd`."

`ae_of_ae_fst`/`ae_of_ae_snd` **live in** `TauCeti/MeasureTheory/Integral/Prod.lean` — a `public
section` / `namespace TauCeti` module whose docstring's stated subject is product-measure helpers.
Hosting the generalised lemma *there* satisfies all three at once and leaves `Compact.lean` needing
exactly the one import `reuse` named. Result: `TauCeti.lintegral_cond_prod_le`, proof **16 → 8**
lines (two transfers + `lintegral_le_const`), parent body still 33.
⇒ **Prospecting signal: read all findings together before fixing any one of them.** Three findings
that each name a different file can still have a single common fix; fixing them one at a time here
would have produced three commits and probably a placement finding in between.

#### ⚠ THE DEFECT MY OWN REVIEW CAUGHT, THAT NO RUBRIC HAD FLAGGED
Moving `ENNReal.ofReal` out of the lemma changed the call site's goal from an **ℝ** inequality to an
**ℝ≥0∞** one, so the round-1 call-site term `(hC x y).trans_eq …` no longer typechecks — it needed
`ENNReal.ofReal_le_ofReal` wrapped around it. Found by re-deriving the goal by hand *because* no
build was available; a build would have caught it in 40 s. **With no compiler, re-elaborate every
goal the generalisation touches, by hand, before pushing** — a type change at the boundary is where
the error lands, not in the moved body.

- **A rubric can flip to green with no push.** #5535's `api-design` went `blocking_request` →
  `green` between two boards at the *same* head with nothing pushed in between. So a blocking state
  is not durable: **re-read the latest board before fixing, or you fix a finding that has already
  been withdrawn.** Sort by `updated_at` and take `last`, never the first board you find.

  (cost one round-trip on #5535).

— a **later** round, since the ledger is append-only — is a substantive **interface DECLINE**:
> "the body is already an ASSEMBLY of four named, commented `have` steps (`hbox`, `hsrc`, `hbij`,

cost a full interface analysis and probably a rejected PR on a target already reasoned out.

review rounds spent against the ten-round budget. But runs 3→5 each demanded a **larger** relocation
than the last, ending by asking to restructure declarations the PR never touched. ⇒ **Stop dry-running
when a run either reverses an earlier approval or asks for work outside the diff.** Ship, and contest
in the real review where a thread exists to reply on — **a dry run has no thread, so a dry-run finding
can only be applied or declined, never contested.**

**⭐⭐ THE GENERALISATION MADE THE LEMMA SHORTER THAN THE BLOCK IT REPLACES — 19 lines inline → an
11-line general lemma.** r133 flagged "state it for an arbitrary `f`, not `expSeries`" as a lesson to
apply up front (after r131/r132 cost two dry-run cycles by not doing so). Applying it paid twice:
- The inline block needed a `let e : Fin (n+1) ≃ Fin (1+n) := finCongr (Nat.add_comm n 1)` **purely
  to reconcile the two spellings of the cardinality**, and composed the bijection with it
  (`(.comp ?_ e.bijective)`, `Function.comp_apply`, `finCongr_apply` in the downstream simp set).
  Stating the lemma over an abstract `ι` **deletes `e` entirely** — there is nothing to reconcile.
- ⇒ **Generalising is not only a rubric-satisfaction move; it removes the adapters a specialised
  statement needs.** Add to the type pre-flight: *does this block carry an equiv/coercion whose only
  job is to match the ambient index type? If so, abstracting the type deletes it.*

**Interface, derived from the block's own body:** the argument is "the card-`m` subsets of a type of
card `m+1` are the singleton complements, and `Finset.piecewise` against such a complement is
`Function.update` at the missing point". Nothing about `expSeries`, `Fin`, or normed algebra. Final
signature takes `(hm : Fintype.card ι = m + 1)` — **the cardinality fact the bijection actually
needs** — rather than a concrete index type. Taking `hm` as a parameter (instead of stating the
subtype as `s.card = Fintype.card ι - 1`) is what lets the consumer's `s.card = n` match
**syntactically**; the `- 1` spelling built fine but would not have unified at the call site.

**Home**: `TauCeti/Data/Finset/Basic.lean` — 28 non-blank lines, subject "cardinality of the nonempty
subsets of a finite type", broadened to "…how many there are, and how to sum over them". Chose an
existing adjacent module over a new one-lemma file (r132 showed api-design pushing toward canonical
homes; this *is* the canonical home for a `Finset` counting/summing fact).

the downstream too); new lemma body **11**; `Exponential.lean` 330 → **311** non-blank;

r144 resolved to try restating in terms of `gammaPDFReal`/`poissonPMFReal` rather than rename a

  `change` failed with *"'change' tactic failed, pattern"*. Introducing `gammaPDFReal` there would

- **`poissonPMFReal (r : ℝ≥0) (n : ℕ)`** is indexed by `ℝ≥0` while the consumer integrates over
  `x : ℝ`, so every point would need wrapping.
⇒ **Resolution: keep the factors expanded and give the lemma a name that claims no API** —
`gammaKernel_mul_exp_mul_pow_div_factorial` (`gammaKernel` was never the rubric's objection; only
`poissonKernel` and `poissonPMF` were). **The docstring now records why the API forms are not used**,
so the next reader — or the next `reuse` finding — does not re-derive it. Build **EXIT 0**.
⇒ **General lesson: when a rubric prescribes "use the real API", try it and let the compiler
adjudicate.** Here the attempt produced the exact evidence needed to justify not doing it, which no
amount of arguing would have. Three renames were wasted precisely because I kept treating a
*statement* problem as a *name* problem.

prime badge.** ⇒ **DECLINE.**

#5592, which reached **10/10**. But **blockprof's output needs a shape check `havescan` gives for
free**: is the block a `have` with its own statement, or a branch? A branch is worth extracting only
when it is *self-contained* — #5592's covariance branch needed **4** binders and no shared preamble;
these need 6 and shared preamble. **Test: does the parent still need the preamble after the cut?
If yes, the branch is not separable.**

**New `documentation` finding on `35e2952f15`** — and it is a real mathematical over-claim, my
sharpest yet. Both docstrings said the identity leaves *"a single gamma kernel of shape `r + k` and
rate `c + 1`"*. Checked against the statement:

```
RHS = c ^ r / (Real.Gamma r * k.factorial) * (x ^ (r + k - 1) * exp (-((c + 1) * x)))
```

The `x`-dependent factor is indeed that of a gamma kernel of shape `r + k`, rate `c + 1` — but such
a kernel is normalised by `(c + 1) ^ (r + k) / Γ (r + k)`, and the surviving constant is
`c ^ r / (Γ r * k !)`. **It is a gamma-kernel-*shaped* factor under the wrong constant.** The rubric
also noted the theorem permits negative `c` and `x` (only `x ≠ 0` is assumed), so "gamma kernel" and
"Poisson weight" are not licensed at all.

> **RULE — a docstring that names a mathematical object is claiming something about the WHOLE
> expression, constant included.** I checked the functional form and stopped. `x ^ (r+k-1) *
> exp(-((c+1)x))` really is a gamma kernel's `x`-part, and that is exactly what made the sentence
> feel true. **Check the constant separately from the shape.** Sixth docstring defect of the
> session; the first that was wrong about *mathematics* rather than about scope or domain.

  them and `attribute [local instance]` does not apply. The `letI`s are forced by the design.

  so `variable`'s usage-based inclusion would have to reproduce the order and explicitness of 5+
  public theorems across two files exactly. That is an API restructure, not a mechanical
  improvement, and its failure mode is silent.

> **RULE — duplication in signatures is not the same target as duplication in proofs.** The ledger's
> note that duplicate blocks "draw unqualified clearance" was about *proof* blocks. Repeated binder
> lists are usually load-bearing (positional API) or forced (hypothesis-dependent instances);

that Mathlib has since deprecated would be a clean, mechanical, one-topic PR. Extracted **3638**
`@[deprecated]` declarations from Mathlib and intersected them with tokens used across the 4321
TauCeti sources: **591 distinct "hits"**, headed by `Finset.sum_congr` (913 uses), `one_ne_zero`
(251), `smul_eq_mul` (754).

**Every one is a false positive.** Checked three against the source:
- `Finset.sum_congr` matched because **`SkewMonoidAlgebra.sum_congr`** is deprecated;
- `one_ne_zero` because **`Ordinal.one_ne_zero`** is;
- `smul_eq_mul` has four live definitions in different namespaces.

My matcher compared **leaf names across namespaces**, so any deprecated `X.foo` condemned every
live `Y.foo`. Lean resolves a name from open namespaces and context, so **no textual match can
decide which declaration a token refers to**.

> **RULE — for anything that depends on name *resolution*, the compiler is the only oracle.** Lean
> emits a deprecation warning at each genuine use; that is the measurement. A grep over leaf names
> is not a weaker version of it, it is a different question with a different answer. This is the
> vendoring-control lesson again in a new costume: I had a control for *"does the name exist"* and
> none for *"is this token that name"*.

> **RULE — a regex over Lean source must mask comments before it matches keywords.** `theorem`,
> `lemma`, `example` all occur in English prose inside docstrings, and TauCeti's docstrings are

ended **mid-expression** — `… gaPointsMulEquiv (R`.

**Cause: named arguments contain `:=`.** `(R := ℤ)` and `(A := A)` are ordinary named arguments
*inside* parentheses, and my line-level `re.search(r':=|\bby\b', l)` matched one and cut the
statement there. Both G2 lemmas truncate at the *same* named argument, producing identical
1099/1100-char prefixes — which is exactly the false "duplicate" pair r171 could not explain.
Depth was being accumulated for the whole line **before** the search, so it never reflected the
match's own position.

only at depth 0. Three controls, all passing:

|---|---|---|
| A — prose `takes` inside a docstring | must be gone | **0** ✔ |
| B — `atkinLehner…_mem_doubleCoset` family | must survive | **6** ✔ |
| C — the false G2 `mul`/`conj` pair | must no longer group | **0** ✔ |

`tools/dupstate.py` is now correct on all three known failure modes (prose, binder-prefix key,

### Corrected a rule from r162 — **`calc` blocks were declined for the wrong reason**
r162 dismissed `calc` rows on *shape*: *"not a `have`; chain, not a step."* Re-examined that, and it
is wrong in principle. A branch's statement must be reconstructed from its context; **a `calc`
block's statement is free — it is the first and last lines.** That makes a `calc` *more* extractable
than a branch, not less.

Read the best-numbered one to test it: `Tannaka/Equivalence.lean:82`
`scalarExtensionComponent_reconstructedPoint_tmul` (36/62, frac 0.58, res 30). Its calc endpoints
mention only `phi, eta, M, m` — **the statement really is free**, as predicted. But the *proof* of
the chain needs `hnatural`, `hf_baseChange_tmul` and `hpointAction`, which need the four `let`s
`D`, `N`, `q`, `f`. A helper must therefore rebuild the entire preamble: parent 62 → ~10,
helper ~55. **Relocate.** Declined — on dependencies, not on shape.

> **CORRECTED RULE — judge a `calc` block on its dependencies alone; its statement costs nothing.**
> The shape gate (`have` vs branch) exists because a branch's *statement* is expensive to recover.
> That reason does not apply to a `calc`, so applying the gate to one is a category error. r162's
> verdict happened to be right for this row and wrong in its reasoning — and a wrong reason
> generalises badly, which is why it is worth correcting even when the outcome does not change.

### Extended `impliedscan` to a new redundancy class: **`≠` implied by a strict inequality**
The order graph modelled `<` and `≤` only. A common and textually decidable pattern it could not
see: `(hx : x ≠ 0)` carried alongside `(hpos : 0 < x)`, where the `≠` is free (`ne_of_gt`).
Added `≠` binders as *targets* (never as edges — a disequality gives no ordering), reported when the
remaining binders provide a **strict** path either way.

**The five known order hits all survive** the change (regression control green).
**New `≠` hits: zero.**

### The firing control is what makes that zero worth reporting
A "no hits" from a matcher that never matches is not a result — that is the r167 deprecated-names
failure. So I measured the matcher itself before believing it:

| measurement | count |
|---|---|
| declarations carrying a `≠` binder | **459** (557 such binders) |
| …of those, also carrying an order/membership binder | **5** |
| …of those, implied by the rest | **0** |

So the matcher fires on 459 declarations — it works — and the pattern is absent for a *structural*
reason: in this codebase a `≠` hypothesis almost never co-occurs with an order hypothesis that
would imply it (5 co-occurrences tree-wide). **The extension is sound and costs nothing, so it stays
in the tool; the finding is that this codebase does not carry that debt.**

> **RULE — a negative result needs a positive control on the matcher, not just on the corpus.**
> r167 reported "591 hits" from a matcher that was wrong; the mirror-image failure is reporting
> "0 hits" from a matcher that never fires. Both are answered the same way: **measure how often the
> pattern's *precondition* occurs.** Here the precondition (a `≠` binder) occurs 459 times and the
> conjunction occurs 5 times — that is what turns "0" from an absence of evidence into evidence of
> absence.

## Round 190 — 08:17Z–08:48Z

### #5628 marked ready 08:17:54Z — CI green, carrying its 10/10 dry run

### `docghost` finished: **255 → 2**, and the tree carries no doc/reachability debt
r189 left five survivors. Read them, and **three more matcher gaps** fell out — each found by
checking one hit against its file, never by counting:

| gap | example | effect |
|---|---|---|
| **`scoped` / `local` modifiers** | `scoped instance instCommGroup (A B : …)` | declaration invisible → false positive |
| **anonymous instances** | `instance : Monoid (RootPairingIsogeny P P) where` — Lean auto-names it `instMonoid`, which appears **nowhere in the source** | unverifiable by text; now skipped rather than reported |
| **trailing-dot prose** | a bullet ending a sentence captured `…ContinuousAmbientIsotopic.` | phantom name |

> **RULE — a name Lean *generates* cannot be checked against source text.** An anonymous
> `instance : Foo` is referred to as `instFoo` in docs and exists nowhere as that string. A textual
> screen must **skip** such names, not report them: reporting is a claim the tool has no way to
> support. (Compare r167: the compiler is the only oracle for name resolution.)

**And the `scoped` fix silently did not apply.** My string replacement did not match the file's
actual wrapping, so the regex was unchanged while the run *looked* successful — the control
(`instCommGroup` must vanish) still showed **1**. Caught by evaluating `DECL` against the literal
source line rather than trusting the edit:

```
NO  -               <- scoped instance instCommGroup (A B : AbelianVariety K) …
OK  instCommGroup   <- instance instCommGroup (A B : X) : CommGroup Y :=
```

> **RULE — verify an edit took effect, do not assume the replacement matched.** A `str.replace`
> that finds nothing changes nothing and raises nothing. The cheap check is to re-derive the
> behaviour from the edited file (here: `exec` the module's header and test the compiled regex),
> which is also what caught it. **Assert on the artifact, not on the intention.**

**Final state: 2 hits of 244**, both the weak class already classified in r189 —
`Submodule.lean` → `SMulMemClass.continuousSMul`, `CartanMap.lean` → `ModuleCat.isFG`: the file
*uses* the name but does not declare it, so the module doc lists what it relies on rather than what
it provides. **Zero instances of the #5579 defect** (advertising a downstream, unreachable
declaration) remain in the tree.

> **The instrument's value here was the negative result, and it took five matcher fixes to earn it.**
> Firing control 17662/17412 (98%); 255 → 14 (reachability) → 6 (prose names) → 5
> (`instance (priority := n)`) → 3 (anonymous instances, trailing dots) → **2** (`scoped`/`local`).

  > before continuing. The symptom (a hang on two small files) looked like catastrophic regex

## Round 201 — 11:18Z–12:15Z

### New capability, and what it is actually good for
r200 restored a clean whole-package build, so per-module rebuilds are now seconds and an **empirical
redundancy test** is available for the first time: *remove a binder, rebuild, keep it if it still
compiles.* That is the elaborator-backed check r167/r173/r191 all concluded was missing.

**Its economics matter, though.** Removing an *instance* binder is source-compatible for callers
(instances are inferred, not passed), so a trial is safe — but proving one needs the defining module
**and its dependents** to compile, i.e. a package build per trial. At ~3 min that is fine for a
handful of candidates and hopeless for hundreds. **The test is a scalpel, not a sieve: it can
confirm a candidate, it cannot find one.**

### Applied it to the `[NeZero]` class from the other worker's #5583 — the class is empty
| measurement | count |
|---|---|
| declarations with ≥1 `[NeZero _]` binder | **333** |
| ...with two or more (the shape #5583 fixed) | **16** |
| ...with a `[NeZero v]` whose `v` appears **nowhere else in the signature** (vacuous binder) | **0** |

The 16 two-binder cases are all on **distinct** variables — `l`/`N`, `d`/`e`, `n`/`m` — so neither
implies the other. Read one rather than assuming:

```lean
lemma heckeTNat_congr {n m : ℕ} [NeZero n] [NeZero m] (h : n = m) :
    heckeTNat (N := N) k n = heckeTNat (N := N) k m := by
  subst h; rfl
```

Both instances are **required by the statement itself**: it mentions `heckeTNat k n` *and*
`heckeTNat k m`, and each application needs its own `NeZero`. The proof being two tokens long makes
the binders look gratuitous; they are not.

> **A short proof is not evidence of redundant hypotheses.** `subst h; rfl` reads like a lemma that
> could not possibly need two instances, and that intuition is exactly backwards: the hypotheses are
> there for the **statement** to elaborate, not for the proof to run. **Check what the statement
> needs before judging binders by the proof's length.**

#5583's own fix was to drop binders that were *derivable in context*, not vacuous — which the
0-of-333 measurement confirms is not textually detectable. Consistent with r167 (name resolution),
r173 (semantic duplication) and r191 (`public import`): **the remaining classes need semantics, and
the empirical test cannot enumerate candidates, only adjudicate them.**

**Round outcome: `no-target`.** open PRs=0, merged=0 this round (**ten this session**), findings=0,

## Round 203 — 11:47Z–12:50Z

**Board:** zero PRs open; main moved `6777fc49b6` → `520c9e5223`, **6 files**. Delta-screened: no

### Found and closed a real hole in my own screening rules
The brief's block-profile table declines `relocate` (largest block ≥ 75% of body) because
*"extraction only moves a long proof."* **That reason fails when the block itself is under 50.**
A body of 58 with a 49-line block gives parent 13 **and** helper 49 — *two* proofs under the bar,
replacing one over it. I have been declining that case categorically since r162.

Measured the class: of **193** proofs with body ≥ 55, exactly **2** are `relocate` with block < 50
and residual < 50:

| candidate | body | largest | frac | → parent / helper |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `CompletelyMonotone/Composition.lean:112` | 58 | 49 | 0.84 | 13 / 49 |
| `Probability/Process/MarkovChain.lean:247` | 55 | 42 | 0.76 | 17 / 42 |

Screens: `Composition.lean` **completely clean** (branchscreen 0 survivors, declinedguard
`no-record`, 0 ledger mentions). `MarkovChain.lean` has two dead fork branches from another lane
(`decompose/markov-prefix-*`, Aug 23–24) — **neither is a PR**, and unlike r186's case the ledger
records no decline, so they are abandoned work rather than a prohibition.

### Both declined — and the reason closes the class
**Both blocks are `induction … with | succ n ih =>` case arms.** Extracting an induction step means
writing the **induction hypothesis as an explicit binder**, and the IH here *is the theorem's own
conclusion* — 3–4 lines of statement plus binders. So:

- `Composition.lean`: helper 49 **+ ~6 lines of IH signature = ~55**, back **over** the bar.
- `MarkovChain.lean`: helper 42 + ~7 = ~49, *just* under — and the parent becomes
  `induction n with | zero => … | succ n ih => exact helper …`, so one 55-line proof becomes an
  8-line proof plus a 49-line one, with the statement duplicated into the helper's signature.
  That is the relocate objection wearing a different hat, and a reviewer would say so.

> **RULE — an induction case arm carries its induction hypothesis into any helper.** The block's
> line count understates the helper by the size of the IH, which for a step lemma is the theorem's
> whole conclusion. **Add the IH to the helper's cost before judging an `induction` arm**, and note
> that this is why the `relocate` gap is empty in practice even though it is real in principle: in
> this tree every member of it is an induction step.

**The hole was still worth finding.** The rule I had been applying — *frac ≥ 0.75 ⇒ decline* — is
wrong as stated, and I applied it about forty times since r162 without noticing. It happened to
reach the right verdict every time because the class it wrongly excludes has two members and both
fail for a different reason. **A rule that is wrong and lucky is still worth correcting**, because
the luck is a property of this tree, not of the rule.

**Round outcome: `no-target`.** open PRs=0, merged=0 (ten this session), findings=0, pushed=0,
opened=0, declined=2, **one screening rule found incorrect, measured, and corrected**,
delta clean, bank empty, next=delta-screen when main moves.

> *"Near-equal top-two blocks ⇒ case split ⇒ shared preamble ⇒ **decline without reading**."*

Measured the class: of 193 proofs with body ≥ 55, **18** have near-equal top-two blocks
(second ≥ 15, gap ≤ max(3, largest/8)). Sampled 8 and read each block's first line — one `sed` per

| block | first line | shape |
|---|---|---|

| `Recut.lean:326` | `· obtain ⟨E, …⟩` | case arm |
| `SimplyConnected.lean:162` | `· have hNr : …` | case arm |
| `Irreducible.lean:179` | `\| E8 =>` | case arm |
| `OverlapOrder.lean:105` | `· have hnot : …` | case arm |
| `StandardBivector.lean:281` | `let rhs : …` | `let` |

**3 of 8 are genuine `have`s.** The rule's premise — that near-equal blocks *are* case arms — is
false in 37% of the sample. r187 generalised from `Recut.lean` alone, and `Recut.lean` is in the
minority-of-one sense the only one I had looked at.

> **RULE CORRECTED — near-equality is weak evidence of a case split, not proof. Always read the
> block's first line; it costs one `sed`.** A rule may say *"this is probably a branch"*; no rule
> may say *"decline without reading"* on the strength of a statistic derived from one instance.

**The verdicts happen to survive**: all three `have`-shaped candidates die on residual —
`RowExchangeable` 222/33 → residual **193**, `GradedCoderivation` 107/29 → **82**,
`Difference` 106/22 → **88**. All are long assembly proofs where no single cut clears the bar. So no
target is lost. **But that is the second consecutive round in which a rule of mine was right by
accident**, and the accident is a property of this tree.

> **Two audits, two wrong rules.** Both were formed at moments when I wanted a cheap way to skip
> work, and both encoded a *correlation* observed once as a *criterion*. The tell is identical in
> each: the rule licenses skipping the very check that would falsify it. **A screening rule that
> forbids an observation is not a screen, it is an assumption** — and while the lane is saturated,

### A real discovery: the tools write their summary to **stderr**
Isolating the above with `2>&1 >/dev/null` printed `# total=0 prime=0 partial=0 relocate=0
assembly=0` — so the totals line goes to **stderr**, not stdout. **Every screen I have run this
session used `2>/dev/null`, which discarded it.** Nothing was corrupted — I read the rows, which are
on stdout — but I have been throwing away the one line that says how much was scanned, and in a
round where a screen returns nothing that line is precisely the firing control I have been
reconstructing by hand (r184, r195).

> **RULE — send `2>/dev/null` only when you know what is on stderr.** I adopted it early to silence
> a noisy tool and then copied it into every screen invocation for ~40 rounds, suppressing the
> summary I later spent whole rounds re-deriving. **A redirection is a decision about information,
> not formatting.**

### The def-mode control caught a design error before the tree did
First `--defs` control run: **hits=0 with both true positives suppressed.** The bucket partition
from r207 — *"no relation symbol ⇒ class-headed ⇒ consumed by instance search"* — was tuned for
**Prop hypotheses**. A `def` parameter `(junk : ℕ)` or `(dead : Type)` is DATA, not an instance, so
the rule suppressed **100% of the true positives in the new population**.

> **A partition calibrated on one population can be exactly wrong on another.** The relational test
> is good evidence about a hypothesis and no evidence at all about a data parameter. Suppression is
> now theorem-only; in `--defs` a class-suspect row is **marked, never hidden**. A screen should
> mark what it cannot verify, not drop it.

### Two more false-positive mechanisms — #10 and #11, both **notation read as name structure**
The first full `--defs` run gave 6 hits; all six were artefacts of `occurs()`, the
identifier-boundary test:

| # | mechanism | evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | **`..` interval notation** | `logIntegral (x : ℝ) := ∫ t in (2 : ℝ)..x, …` — my projection guard rejects any occurrence preceded by `.`, which also rejects `..x`. Also `halfLinePrimitive`, `integratedLaplaceKernel` |
| 11 | **postfix modifier letters** | `enlargeRow … := (enlargeColumn Vᵀ η)ᵀ` and `supportedPart … := … Sᶜ` — `ᵀ`/`ᶜ` are Unicode category **Lm**, which `isalnum()` accepts, so `V`/`S` looked like prefixes of longer names |

Fixes: a `.` marks a projection **only when an identifier precedes the dot** (`f.symm` yes, `2..x`
no); and category-`Lm` characters are excluded from the identifier class while **subscripts stay
in**, because `h₀` really is one name. Controlled both ways — `ctl_projection_still_rejected`
verifies `g.symm` is still handled.

> **The four cheap-key bugs (r167/r170/r172/r173) were about keys; these two are about notation.**
> `Vᵀ`, `Sᶜ`, `2..x` are operators wearing name characters. **When a scanner reasons about
> identifier boundaries in Lean, enumerate the postfix notation before trusting `isalnum`.**

**Eleven false-positive mechanisms now documented for one instrument, and it reports zero.** The
zero is worth exactly as much as the mechanisms behind it: without them the same scan reported 128,
then 6, and every one would have been a wasted PR.

6 of 27 surviving means **78% disqualified**. That is high enough to be worth a look, and the look
found it: the tactic filter was `any(t in body.lower() for t in CTX)` — a **substring** test.

- `"order"` fires on `Ordered`, `IsOrderedRing`, `reorder`
- `"trivial"` fires on `Nontrivial` — and lowercasing makes this unavoidable

8 of 44 entries are substring-dangerous. Replaced with a token match carrying the same
identifier-boundary logic as `occurs()` (and refusing a preceding `.`, so `Foo.trivial` is a term,
not a tactic); literals with punctuation (`simp [*`, `exact?`, `assumption'`) stay substring tests.

|---|---|---|---|

> **A filter that over-fires is invisible in the output — only the precondition count reveals it.**
> Nothing about `hits=0` could have told me a third of the disqualifications were bogus; the
> **78%-on-27** ratio in a five-file delta is what did. r184's rule ("a screen that can return zero
> must print its own precondition count") was written to prove a screen *fired*. It just did
> something better: it caught a bug in the screen's own logic.

> **Match a tactic as a token, never a substring** — and never on lowercased text, where
> `Nontrivial` becomes `nontrivial`.

**The zero now rests on 34,837 fully-screened declarations rather than 29,303**, which is the whole
value of the round: same conclusion, 19% more evidence, and one fewer way for the instrument to be

### Three self-inflicted bugs in the deletion script — all caught by asserting on the artifact
The scan was sound; my *editing* was not. None of these would have been caught by reading the
intention.

1. **`omit` missing from the body terminator set.** `omit [...] in` binds to the *next*
   declaration, so it ends the previous body. Without it the cut ran past the target and swallowed
   the **following** declaration's `omit` line — silently changing `jetField_smul_ae`'s typeclass
   assumptions. This is r207's mechanism #9 recurring, and **`omit` was sitting in r207's own
   vocabulary table at 11 occurrences, where I wrote it off as "a command, not a tactic — not
   relevant".**
2. **`\b` after the whole alternation disabled `/-` and `@[`.** A word boundary cannot hold between
   `-` and `!`, so `/-!` and `/--` stopped terminating the scan and three cuts ran into the *next*
   declaration's docstring. Anchored `\b` to the word alternatives only.
3. Attempted `git checkout -- TauCeti` to reset — **blocked by the Lean guardrail hook**, correctly.
   Rewrote each file from `git show origin/main:<path>` instead.

Only after adding an **assertion that each removed block contains exactly one declaration** did all
ten come out right, followed by a structural check of every modified file (balanced `/-`…`-/`, no
consecutive or stranded `omit`): 10/10 clean.

> **A verified finding does not make the edit that acts on it verified.** The screen was
> control-verified over four rounds; the twenty lines of deletion logic I wrote in one go had three
> defects, two of which changed code I never intended to touch. **Assert on the edit with the same
> discipline as on the screen** — the "exactly one declaration per removed block" assertion is what
> converted a plausible diff into a correct one.

### Three string-patches produced a file whose structure I no longer knew
The first attempt patched `deadprivate.py` in place: the replacement text contained module-level

> **A syntax check is not a structure check.** Three successive `str.replace` patches left `scan()`

> `def` boundaries, read the resulting outline (`grep -n '^def '`) — or rewrite the file.**

> printed on the search succeeding, not on the edit landing. This is r190 again, in the reporting
> rather than the edit.

### New instrument `redundantimport.py` — imports another import already provides
Purely syntactic, decidable from the tree, and named by the `placement` rubric ("evidently unused
or overly broad import"). The whole difficulty is one semantic fact:

> **Under the module system an import is NOT transitive.** `import B` gives you B; B's own plain
> imports stay private to B. Only `public import` re-exports. So "A is redundant because B imports
> it" holds precisely along chains of **public** imports. This repo: **6,582 public + 1,219 plain**
> TauCeti edges — and one file's own prose says *"import is not public, so this adds no second
> route"*. Ignoring the distinction would have reported most of the tree.

Two rules, deliberately asymmetric: a **plain** `import A` is covered if *any* other direct import
publicly reaches A (the file only needs to *see* A); a **`public import A`** is covered only if
another **public** import publicly reaches A (the file also *re-exports* A). Controlled both ways —
the discriminating fixture, a cover that imports the target *plainly*, is correctly spared.

### 431 → 8, and every filter was earned by a wrong row
| stage | rows | why |
|---|---|---|
| raw redundancy | **431** | transitively available |
| − roll-up/index modules | −17 | a file that declares nothing IS its import list; removing "duplicates" there destroys the file's purpose |
| − module's names referenced | −… | the file uses A directly; removing the import makes a real dependency implicit |
| − instance/notation providers | −5 | **`Tangent/FiniteType.lean` declares exactly one thing: `instance instModuleFiniteCotangentSpace`.** An instance is consumed by typeclass search and never named, so "no name referenced" is not "unused" |
| **kept** | **8** | banked in `r218-redundantimport-bank.txt` |

> **"Transitively available" is not "redundant", and "no name referenced" is not "unused".** Both
> substitutions look sound and both are false — the second failed on the *first* module I checked
> by hand. This is the r211 pattern again (an "unused private" that exists to be elaborated): **a
> screen names a syntactic property; the defect is a semantic one, and the gap between them is
> where every false positive lives.**

> **A useful property of this class:** removing a transitively-available import **cannot break the
> build** — the file still sees the module through its cover, and for a `public import` the cover
> re-exports it. So the risk here is a rubric objection, never a red CI. That inverts the usual
> gating: the dry run matters more than the build.

**Round outcome: `maintained`.** open=1, merged=0, findings=0, pushed=0, opened=0, **new instrument
`redundantimport.py` with controls; 431→8 banked**, next=read the scoreboard for `0fdebcbb59`;
re-drive past 16:05Z if absent; then verify 2–3 bank rows by hand and open a focused PR.

|---|---|---|

| identical NAME twice in one file | 38 | Lean forbids that in one namespace, so these are **different namespace blocks** |

> wall: r173 (`dupstate`, semantic duplication), r222 (imports needed for elaboration), and now

> what is in scope.**

### `dupbinder.py` — the last member of the scope-constant family, and a controlled zero
r225 gave the principle: when a screen is blocked by scope, find a class where **scope is
constant**. Inside a single signature everything shares one namespace, one `variable` block and one
local context, so two binders with identical type text really are the same hypothesis. Built it.

**Result: `duplicates=0` across 57,188 declarations**, 30,302 of which carry 2+ comparable binders,
both positive controls firing. **TauCeti has no declaration with a redundantly repeated
hypothesis.**

### Getting there took FOUR corrections, all one root
| # | correction | evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | data binders of the same type are **normal** | my control *expected* `{s : Set α} {t : Set α}` to fire — you need two sets. **The expectation was the error, not the code.** |
| 2 | length guard `>= 6` suppressed a real hit | `s ⊆ t` is 5 characters |
| 3 | `→`, `≃`, `≅` are **type-forming**, not relations | including them took 17 hits to **66**, every new row a data binder: `ℝ → ℂ` is a curve, `α ≃ β` a type of equivalences |
| 4 | a relational glyph must be **space-delimited** | `ℝ≥0` embeds `≥` in NOTATION; two of them are two numbers. 66 → 2 → **0** |

> **"Contains a relational glyph" is a proxy for "is a Prop", and the proxy leaks — on type-forming
> operators and on notation that embeds a relational character.** I have used this proxy since r207
> without stress-testing it; building a second instrument on it is what exposed the leaks.

### The same proxy, two questions, two opposite correct answers
Checked whether `unusedscan` shares the leak: it uses the same glyph set with no space-delimiting,
so `ℝ≥0` classes as relational there too. **It is not a defect there.** The two instruments ask
different questions:

* `unusedscan`: *can typeclass search consume this binder?* `ℝ≥0` is data → **no** → report it.
  **Correct.**
* `dupbinder`: *is this a proposition that could be redundantly repeated?* `ℝ≥0` is data → **no** →
  must not report it. The proxy said yes. **Wrong.**

> **A shared test is not a shared judgement.** r209 said a partition calibrated on one population
> can be wrong on another; this is sharper — the *same* test on the *same* input is right in one
> instrument and wrong in the other, because the question differs. **Before reusing a predicate,

### Measured my own measure of worth for the first time
The identity names **review rounds per PR** as the measure, and the whole dry-run discipline is
justified by it — but I have asserted the payoff for 200 rounds without computing it. Read the
`full_rounds` field from the final scoreboard of every `improve/*` PR merged in this session.

**14 merged PRs, 33 review rounds, mean 2.36** (cap is 10, each round ~1 hour).

**The distribution matters far more than the mean:**

| | PRs | rounds | |
|---|---|---|---|
| **≥4 rounds** | 4 (29%) | **19 (58%)** | #5576 (**7**), #5579 (4), #5618 (4), #5590 (4) |
| **<4 rounds** | 10 (71%) | 14 | mean **1.40** |

There is **no improvement trend over time** — first four merged average 1.25, last four average
2.00. The cost is not a learning curve; it is concentrated in a *kind* of PR.

**What the expensive four have in common:** every one asserts a **judgement**. #5576 claimed a proof
was the right shape and drew three successive `reuse` citations, each naming a better existing
lemma. #5579 moved a declaration and had to re-argue its placement. #5618 claimed seven hypotheses
were implied. #5590 promoted a lemma's generality.

**What the cheap ones have in common:** their claim is **checkable**. #5655 — *these declarations
are unreferenced*. #5663 — *this import is reachable along a public chain*. #5583 — *this instance
is shadowed*. Both of the deletion PRs built from this session's own instruments landed in
**1 round each**.

> **A PR's cost is set by whether its central claim is checkable or arguable**, not by its size or
> its subject. #5663 touched 8 files and cost 1 round; #5576 touched one declaration and cost 7.
> This is r219's *"when a claim is provable, prove it"* with a number attached: **judgement PRs cost
> ~4.75 rounds, checkable PRs ~1.4.**

**Forward consequence:** when two candidate classes are available, prefer the one whose claim a
reviewer can *verify* rather than *weigh*. And **#5671 is a judgement PR** — "this block deserves a
name" — so expect more than one round despite its all-ten-green dry run. That is calibration, not
pessimism: it makes the dry run more valuable, not less.

**Round outcome: `maintained`.** open=1, merged=0, findings=0, pushed=0, opened=0, delta clean,
**review-rounds-per-PR quantified for the first time (2.36 mean; 58% of cost in 29% of PRs)**,
next=poll merges; re-drive #5671 only past ~19:41Z if still unscored.

### Acted on r232's finding — and killed a class before it cost anything
r232 measured that **checkable** claims cost ~1.4 review rounds and **arguable** ones ~4.75, so the
right move with spare capacity is to look for another checkable class. Two candidates:

* **shadowed instances** (the shape of #5583, which merged in 1 round) — `nsshadow` screens
  *namespace* shadowing and its candidate set is already exhausted (it produced #5628). An
  *instance* shadowed by a more general one requires instance resolution: **not textually
  screenable.** Declined.
* **orphan modules** — "nothing imports this file" is as checkable as a claim gets, and it reuses
  the import graph built for `redundantimport`.

**The orphan screen fired hard: 881 of 4384 modules (20%) are imported by nothing.** Twenty percent
is remarkable, so per r199 I looked for the measurement bug instead of the PR — **and the repo
answers the question directly.** `TauCeti.lean` says of itself:

> *"It is intentionally empty. The lakefile's `globs = ["TauCeti.*"]` is authoritative for what gets
> built … `lake build` builds every `TauCeti/` module directly … No code does `import TauCeti`."*

Confirmed in `lakefile.toml`: `globs = ["TauCeti.*"]`. **Every module is a build root**, so a module
nothing imports is a *library leaf* — the normal terminal state for results in a mathematics
library — not dead code. **The class is void, not merely empty.**

> **Before inferring deadness from an import graph, read the build configuration that decides what
> counts as a root.** `deadprivate` was sound because `private` scope is a *language* fact; module
> reachability is a *build-system* fact, and the build system here makes every file reachable. The
> same reasoning — "nothing references it, so it is dead" — is valid in one case and vacuous in the
> other.

Cost of checking: two commands. Cost of not checking: a PR proposing to delete 881 modules.

### Built `tools/controls.sh` — and it was broken in the way that matters most
Every instrument has been patched since its controls were written (`dupsig` twice, `deadprivate`
three times), and r216 showed a patch can leave a file that parses and is wrong. There was no way
to check them as a suite. Wrote one: **11 assertions over 6 instruments**, each naming the rows it
expects, plus **negative** assertions naming rows that must NOT appear (`deadprivate` spares
attributed and dot-notation-used declarations; `dupbinder` spares data binders; `redundantimport`
spares a plainly-imported cover; `unusedscan` spares context-consuming proofs).

**The first version printed `0 passed, 0 failed` while all 11 checks passed** — every `chk` is
invoked through a **pipe**, so it runs in a subshell and `pass=$((pass+1))` is discarded when that
subshell exits. Its exit status was therefore `success` regardless of results.

> **A control suite that cannot fail is worse than none**, because it converts "unverified" into
> "verified" without doing any work. Results now go to a temp file, and the exit status requires
> `failures == 0` **and** `passes > 0` — so an empty run fails too.

**Then controlled the control suite**: deliberately broke `dupsig` (raised its group threshold to
99), re-ran, and confirmed **10 passed, 1 failed, exit 1**; restored and confirmed **11 passed,
exit 0**. Without that step "11 passed" is a claim, not a measurement.

**Twice this round I read `$?` through a pipe** and got `tail`'s status instead of the script's —
the first time it hid the very failure I was testing for. Verified the exit codes with the pipe
removed.

> **`$?` after a pipeline is the last command's status, not the one you care about.** Same shape as
> r205's `2>/dev/null` eating a firing control: the shell reported on the wrong thing and the
> reading looked fine.

## Round 263 — 02:47Z–02:50Z

**Board:** 0 open, 15 merged since 09-03T23:42. Main `79cffcb88c` → `f8e9ff1f61`, 1 file
(`Huber/LocalizationTopology/Basic.lean`).

### A live delta hit exposed a real defect in `dupsig`
The delta reported **6 declarations sharing one signature**, same file, same namespace, unlabelled —
i.e. presented as a genuine finding. But their names (`isOpen_locSubring`, `isBounded_locSubring`,
`hasBasis_nhds_zero_locSubring`, `isAdic_locIdeal`, …) are plainly *different statements*. Six
identical signatures would be remarkable, so per r199 I looked for the measurement bug.

**Mechanism — a statement-level `letI`.** These theorems read

```
theorem isOpen_locSubring … (hden : HasDenominatorPower P T s S) :
    letI := locTopology P T s S hden
    IsOpen (locSubring P T s S : Set S) := by
```

The `letI :=` sits at **bracket depth 0**, so `top_level_assign` stopped there and every signature
was truncated to the shared binders plus that identical `letI` line — before the conclusions
diverge. **Depth-awareness (r236's fix for `(X := X)`) cannot catch this**; the third variant of the
r172 cheap-key family for one function.

**Not a corner case: the shape occurs 779 times in the tree.**

**Two fixes.** (1) `top_level_assign` skips a depth-0 `:=` on a line beginning `letI`/`haveI`/`let`/
`have`. (2) The chunk gather now reads until a *real* terminator exists rather than until any `:=`
appears — without this, the fix converted the false positive into a **silent drop** of all 779.

**Controlled both ways** (r237): with the fix, a `letI`-shaped pair with differing conclusions is
distinguished and a real duplicate still collides; **with the fix deliberately reverted, the bogus
collision reappears** with sig `… : letI`. The first fixture I wrote put `letI` mid-line and did not
exercise the mechanism at all — corrected before trusting it.

**Effect tree-wide:**

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| distinct signatures | 45,318 | **48,030** (+2,712 no longer collapsed) |
| collision groups | 267 | **224** |
| **unlabelled** (needing a human read) | 104 | **68** |

The delta's own file now reports **55 declarations, 55 distinct signatures, 0 groups**.

> **Instrument defects surface from live data, not from audits.** Rounds 241–249 audited this
> instrument's coverage, records and controls and found it sound; a single unusual file found a bug
> that had been mis-collapsing 2,712 signatures the whole time. **An audit checks what you thought
> to check; the delta checks what the tree actually contains.**

Other five instruments clean (62 declarations, 6 private). **Whole-tree `redundantimport`:** 4406
modules, `426 redundant`, hash-identical → KEEP 3 / NEW 0. Ninth consecutive snapshot at 426.

**Round outcome: `no-target`.** open=0, merged=0, findings=0, pushed=0, opened=0, **`dupsig`
truncation defect found from live data and fixed; 2,712 signatures un-collapsed**,
next=delta-screen when main moves.
